builder_plan.scenario: A self-hosted assistant is too expensive because its model uses most of the GPU memory.
builder_plan.change: Try the paper's supported lower-precision weights on a copy of your serving setup.
builder_plan.baseline: The same model at its original precision, on the same GPU.
steps: Locate the paper's implementation and check its license, model support, data needs, and hardware requirements. Stop here if you cannot obtain the required artifacts.
Save a small set of representative product tasks and expected outcomes. Keep evaluation tasks out of any training or tuning, and choose quality and cost limits before running.
Run the baseline and the proposed change on identical inputs. Keep other settings fixed and repeat paired runs to expose variation.
Save per-task outputs, failures, timings, and all usage costs. Review regressions before expanding the test.
builder_plan.measure: Peak memory, task pass rate, latency, and total serving cost at the same context and load.
builder_plan.decision: Keep the change only if it meets your preselected quality and latency limits and improves the metric you care about after setup and operating costs. Otherwise retain the baseline. This is an exploration plan, not a validated recommendation.

title: Integer-Quantized Hierarchical Matrices with Adaptive Bit Allocation
summary: The method replaces FP64 dense or FP64 low-rank-factor storage of hierarchical matrices (kernel and BEM matrices) with integer-quantized low-rank factors whose bitwidths are greedily allocated per singular value under a reconstruction error budget. It costs an offline discrete optimization and quantization pass plus controlled approximation error bounded by the chosen budget, and it adds implementation complexity in the hierarchical partition and error analysis. It can fail when blocks are not compressible (low-rank structure absent), when the truncation and reconstruction error bounds eta_k and R_k are misestimated, or when downstream solvers are sensitive to the induced max-norm errors.
rationale: The technique targets storage compression of dense kernel and boundary-element matrices in numerical linear algebra, not LLM weights, activations, or inference, so it falls outside an ML engineer's production adoption scope unless they operate scientific-computing solvers.
technique: Adaptive bitwidth quantization of hierarchical low-rank matrix factors

claims.statement: The method replaces FP64 dense or FP64 low-rank-factor storage of hierarchical matrices (kernel and BEM matrices) with integer-quantized low-rank factors whose bitwidths are greedily allocated per singular value under a reconstruction error budget. It costs an offline discrete optimization and quantization pass plus controlled approximation error bounded by the chosen budget, and it adds implementation complexity in the hierarchical partition and error analysis. It can fail when blocks are not compressible (low-rank structure absent), when the truncation and reconstruction error bounds eta_k and R_k are misestimated, or when downstream solvers are sensitive to the induced max-norm errors.
Up to 44.3x storage reduction versus dense FP64 storage and up to 5.70x versus FP64 low-rank factors, with reconstruction errors below the specified max-norm bounds in all hierarchical tests.
